bibl.title: Toward a theory of media priming
bibl.publisher: Annals of the International Communication Association

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Media priming operates entirely within System 1 processing (fast, automatic, and with little effort) and should only include effects of a prime that are beyond the conscious awareness of the media consumer.

span.label: media priming
span.quote: The argument presented here is that media priming occurs when the response to some aspect of media content – the influence of the prime – happens outside the media consumer’s awareness.

span.label: review
span.quote: This paper begins by detailing the existing definitions of priming, focusing on the different uses of ‘priming’ within media research and its overlap with other media theories.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A prime spreads activation through an associative memory network, and because only a few activated nodes reach conscious awareness the resulting judgment cannot be traced back to its source.
span.quote: Priming operates through the associative activation of memory, where information can trigger the activation of other ideas from memory in a ‘cascade of activity’ (Kahneman, 2011, p. 51).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Media priming works by activating nodes or networks of nodes in associative memory outside the media consumer's immediate awareness.
span.quote: Media priming then relies on the use of associative memory, where nodes (or networks of nodes) are activated outside the media consumer’s immediate awareness.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Awareness cancels the effect: once people notice the prime or deliberate about the source of their decision they correct for it, which is why the effect requires unawareness.
span.quote: Providing further evidence of this proposition, prior research has found that when participants carefully consider the impact of information, the source of their decisions, and/or are made aware of the priming mechanism, they are less likely to be influenced by the prime because they will correct for it (Lepore & Brown, 2002; Lombardi et al., 1987; Thompson et al., 1994).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A gap between desired and actual confidence in a political judgment motivates a switch from System 1 to System 2, which is why evaluations of political actors can be made within awareness.
span.quote: If the desired level of confidence is not reached, System 2 would be activated, as System 2 is necessary when one’s desired level of confidence in their judgement is not the same as their actual level of confidence.

span.label: The paper sets aside the argument that System 1 / System 2 dichotomisation is itself inadequate, treating it as out of scope.
span.quote: Though this argument is beyond the scope of this paper, it should be noted that priming should occur within System 1 (or other versions of unconscious processing, see below) even if that processing began as intentional and shifted to unaware, for example.

span.label: The paper imports the dual-process account of cognition wholesale and uses it as the machinery for distinguishing media priming from political priming in communication research.
span.quote: It then applies dualprocess models to the study of priming to illustrate the cognitive processing that occurs within media priming (and political priming).

span.label: Chooses Kahneman's and Stanovich and West's System 1 / System 2 vocabulary, in preference to the communication field's own ELM and HSM, as the framework for the new theory.
span.quote: Given that the System 1 and System 2 description encapsulates many of the propositions put forth in the ELM, the HSM, and other dual-process models, it will be utilized here.

span.label: media priming
span.quote: the theory of media priming put forth here posits that media priming can only occur within System 1, where it takes place when a media stimulus causes some reaction that occurs for reasons outside the media consumer’s awareness. Media priming then relies on the use of associative memory, where nodes (or networks of nodes) are activated outside the media consumer’s immediate awareness. The media consumer is influenced by some aspect of that media content, but they are unable to mentally trace the source of said influence.

span.label: political priming
span.quote: On the other hand, political priming, as described above, is a process that can occur within the individual’s awareness and can involve a clear and traceable cognitive connection that originates from an external source.

span.label: System 1
span.quote: Stanovich and West (2000) defined System 1 as ‘automatic, largely unconscious, and relatively undemanding of computational capacity

span.label: System 2
span.quote: Kahneman (2011) defined System 2 as allocating ‘attention to the effortful mental activities that demand it

span.label: agenda setting
span.quote: That is, political priming, in particular, can act as an extension of agenda setting, which is in line with previous scholars’ arguments in terms of an accessibility-based perspective of political news effects.

span.label: prime
span.quote: At its most basic level, priming is the presentation of a stimulus and the effects caused by that stimulus, which can include subsequent changes in beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors. A prime, then, is the portion of the stimulus that leads to these effects.

span.label: awareness
span.quote: Scholars have also specified that an awareness of the stimulus itself is not the crucial point to consider in priming research (Bargh, 2016). Instead, an awareness of the influence or potential influence of the prime(s) within the stimulus is what matters.

span.label: learning
span.quote: After testing the occurrence of learning – as opposed to priming – as the explanation of ‘political priming’ effects, Lenz (2009) argued that these findings did not show evidence of priming; rather, they were evidence of news consumers learning about some of the issues covered by the media.

span.label: priming, at its most basic - the presentation of a stimulus and the effects it causes, with the PRIME separated out as the portion of the stimulus responsible. The paper starts from the least contested version and then shows it does not survive contact with the field
span.quote: At its most basic level, priming is the presentation of a stimulus and the effects caused by that stimulus, which can include subsequent changes in beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors. A prime, then, is the portion of the stimulus that leads to these effects.

span.label: priming per Bargh 2016, quoted at length as the best available clarification - PASSIVE, UNINTENDED, and not accurately reportable. The definition works by exclusion: an explicit instruction is not priming because the person intends it, and presenting new information is LEARNING rather than passive activation of what is already in the head
span.quote: Priming effects of recent experience on presently made responses to that environment (judgments, verbal and nonverbal behavior, actions) are passive effects that the individual did not intend to occur, and of which influence the individual is not aware and cannot accurately verbally report upon. This separates priming effects from just any effect of recent experience. Task instructions to think or feel or behave in a certain way — logically, mindfully, compassionately, thoughtfully — are cases of explicit instruction (so the person is aware of and intends to think that way — not priming), or of presenting new information to the participant (which is learning and not passive activation of what is already in the person’s head — not priming).

span.label: media priming, the paper's own sense - restricted to System 1 and defined by the consumer's INABILITY TO TRACE the influence. A sense drawn as a limit on an existing word rather than a new mechanism
span.quote: the theory of media priming put forth here posits that media priming can only occur within System 1, where it takes place when a media stimulus causes some reaction that occurs for reasons outside the media consumer’s awareness. Media priming then relies on the use of associative memory, where nodes (or networks of nodes) are activated outside the media consumer’s immediate awareness. The media consumer is influenced by some aspect of that media content, but they are unable to mentally trace the source of said influence.

span.label: political priming, the sense inherited from agenda setting - media coverage makes an issue salient and the consumer then weighs it when judging a politician. The paper's point is that this can be a CONSCIOUS application, which is what puts it outside media priming
span.quote: On the other hand, political priming, as described above, is a process that can occur within the individual’s awareness and can involve a clear and traceable cognitive connection that originates from an external source.

span.label: awareness, as the paper narrows it - NOT awareness of the stimulus but awareness of the INFLUENCE of the prime within it. The narrowing is what makes the boundary testable, because a consumer can watch an advertisement knowingly and still be primed by it
span.quote: Scholars have also specified that an awareness of the stimulus itself is not the crucial point to consider in priming research (Bargh, 2016). Instead, an awareness of the influence or potential influence of the prime(s) within the stimulus is what matters.

span.label: the operational test for the boundary, which is the part most definitional papers omit: ask whether the participant can identify the prime, and if they can, the study is not studying media priming
span.quote: If the media consumer is able to identify the prime within the media stimulus that influenced their response to it, then it would not be considered media priming.

span.label: builds-on → Bargh (2016)
span.quote: Toward this end, perhaps the best clarification of what constitutes priming was provided by Bargh (2016) in his recent summary of priming research:

span.label: builds-on → Kahneman (2011)
span.quote: In this way, Kahneman (2011) explicitly and unambiguously placed priming within System 1.

span.label: builds-on → Roskos-Ewoldsen et al. (2007, 2009)
span.quote: Scholars have made explicit calls for the need for greater distinction in the use of priming within media research (e.g. Roskos-Ewoldsen et al., 2009; Roskos-Ewoldsen et al., 2007), and this paper seeks to address these concerns.

span.label: builds-on → Lenz (2009)
span.quote: Political priming, on the other hand, may occur when information is processed within System 2, where individuals can trace the connection between the information within media content and the subsequent effect of that information (see Lenz, 2009, for a clear description of this process).

span.label: media priming —part-of→ System 1
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — The core proposal, and it is stated as a restriction - `can only occur within System 1` - so the edge is a containment rather than a cause.
span.quote: the theory of media priming put forth here posits that media priming can only occur within System 1, where it takes place when a media stimulus causes some reaction that occurs for reasons outside the media consumer’s awareness. Media priming then relies on the use of associative memory, where nodes (or networks of nodes) are activated outside the media consumer’s immediate awareness. The media consumer is influenced by some aspect of that media content, but they are unable to mentally trace the source of said influence.

span.label: political priming —part-of→ System 2
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — WEIGHTED FOR ITS OWN HEDGING. The paper says `entirely plausible`, not demonstrated, and immediately concedes System 1 remains possible. What it does assert is the consequence: only one of the two routes fits the theory.
span.quote: Therefore, while it is possible that political priming could occur through System 1 processing, it is also entirely plausible that it could occur through System 2 processing. These would represent different psychological processes, only one of which would fit within the theory of media priming presented here.

span.label: political priming —distinct-from→ media priming
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE PROCESSING HAPPENS INSIDE THE CONSUMER'S AWARENESS - both may run on accessibility, and that shared mechanism is exactly why the two have been treated as one thing · strength of the relation: 0.9 — The paper's central separation, and it grants the similarity before drawing the line: same accessibility mechanism, different awareness.
span.quote: While both media priming and political priming could operate through cognitive accessibility, as previous research has suggested, media priming involves processing that occurs outside the individuals’ awareness, while political priming could involve processing that takes place within the individual’s awareness.

span.label: political priming —part-of→ agenda setting
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — Attributed to a long list of media-effects scholars rather than argued here, and hedged with `can act as` - hence 0.7. It is the genealogy that explains why one field has two incompatible senses of one word.
span.quote: That is, political priming, in particular, can act as an extension of agenda setting, which is in line with previous scholars’ arguments in terms of an accessibility-based perspective of political news effects.

span.label: learning —distinct-from→ political priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — Lenz's charge, reported by this paper: the political-priming findings were consumers LEARNING which issues the media covered. If that is right the effect leaves the priming category altogether rather than moving to the other side of this paper's boundary - a third option the System 1 / System 2 split does not provide for.
span.quote: After testing the occurrence of learning – as opposed to priming – as the explanation of ‘political priming’ effects, Lenz (2009) argued that these findings did not show evidence of priming; rather, they were evidence of news consumers learning about some of the issues covered by the media.

span.label: prime —distinct-from→ awareness
span.note: differs in: WHICH OBJECT THE AWARENESS IS OF: of the stimulus, which may be fully conscious, versus of the prime's influence, which must not be · strength of the relation: 0.9 — The distinction that makes the theory testable rather than merely restrictive - a viewer can knowingly watch the content and still be primed by an element of it.
span.quote: Scholars have also specified that an awareness of the stimulus itself is not the crucial point to consider in priming research (Bargh, 2016). Instead, an awareness of the influence or potential influence of the prime(s) within the stimulus is what matters.

span.label: The paper proposes that media priming, properly defined, occurs only within System 1 processing, when a media stimulus produces a reaction whose source the consumer cannot trace.
span.quote: Given these considerations, the theory of media priming put forth here posits that media priming can only occur within System 1, where it takes place when a media stimulus causes some reaction that occurs for reasons outside the media consumer’s awareness.

span.label: Media priming and political priming are separated by awareness rather than by accessibility: the first works outside awareness, the second may work inside it.
span.quote: While both media priming and political priming could operate through cognitive accessibility, as previous research has suggested, media priming involves processing that occurs outside the individuals’ awareness, while political priming could involve processing that takes place within the individual’s awareness.

span.label: Political priming is argued to be plausibly a System 2 phenomenon and therefore a different psychological process from media priming.
span.quote: Therefore, while it is possible that political priming could occur through System 1 processing, it is also entirely plausible that it could occur through System 2 processing.

span.label: The review identifies two divergent research camps using the same word 'priming' with different operationalizations and different effect patterns.
span.quote: Beyond these basic definitional similarities, two broad camps have developed within media research with quite different operationalizations and findings.

span.label: The theory yields a testable criterion: a manipulation check establishing that the consumer cannot identify the prime is required before the label media priming applies.
span.quote: If the media consumer is able to identify the prime within the media stimulus that influenced their response to it, then it would not be considered media priming.

span.label: Applying the criterion to an existing study of terrorism news framing shows it does not qualify as media priming because participants demonstrably noticed the manipulated phrase.
span.quote: Due to participants’ clear awareness of the information included in the news story and its application to their judgments, this example would not be illustrative of media priming (appropriately, the authors discuss their findings in terms of equivalence framing).

span.label: media priming
span.quote: This manuscript puts forth a theory of media priming, where media priming occurs when information from media content is utilized outside the media consumer’s awareness.

span.label: priming (basic definition)
span.quote: At its most basic level, priming is the presentation of a stimulus and the effects caused by that stimulus, which can include subsequent changes in beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors.

span.label: prime
span.quote: A prime, then, is the portion of the stimulus that leads to these effects.

span.label: political priming
span.quote: More simply put, political priming is the process them all through which media coverage of an issue increases the weight placed upon it by the media consumer, which then is used in evaluating a politician or political party (Iyengar & Kinder, 1987).

span.label: System 1
span.quote: Stanovich and West (2000) defined System 1 as ‘automatic, largely unconscious, and relatively undemanding of computational capacity’ (p. 658).

span.label: System 2
span.quote: Kahneman (2011) defined System 2 as allocating ‘attention to the effortful mental activities that demand it’ (p. 21).

span.label: law of least effort
span.quote: Given this law of least effort (Bohner et al., 1995; Kahneman, 2011), System 1 processing is more likely to occur than System 2 processing.

span.label: sufficiency principle
span.quote: This proposition fits within the sufficiency principle, where individuals seek balance between using the least amount of effort and having confidence in their attitudes and decisions (Bohner et al., 1995).
